newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Prague PSE says 1996 volume doubled but mostly OTC.
newsitem.headline: Prague PSE says 1996 volume doubled but mostly OTC.

text.p: Turnover on the Prague Stock Exchange (PSE) doubled in 1996 to 393.1 billion crowns ($14.5 billion) from 195.4 billion the previous year, a bourse report said.

But the PSE report said trades conducted on the its automated central market had declined as a percentage of overall trading activity, with the overwhelming majority taking place in over-the-counter block trades.
It said 1996 turnover on the automated market totalled just 28.77 billion crowns, up from 21.99 billion in 1995, but far below the overall rate of growth on the market.

In the report, given to government ministers in December and presented to journalists on Thursday, the PSE said activity on its central market dropped to just two percent of all 1996 securities trading from about 10 percent two years ago.

It said weak regulation and OTC trades registered on the Central Securities Registry (SCP) hindered building confidence in the equities market, where key indices rose roughly 20 percent in 1996 compared with 80 percent in Poland and 135 percent in Hungary.

The PSE said 57 percent of the 1.088 trillion crowns in 1996 Czech securities trading was simply registered at the SCP where individual trades are not publicly disclosed, making pricing transparency difficult.
It said roughly seven percent of trades were on the small investor-oriented RM-System, while the PSE conducted or registered 35.73 percent of all 1996 Czech trades.
PSE Chairman Tomas Jezek said he believed that a long-awaited independent markets watchdog would be created by July in an effort to bring more confidence to the market.
"As regards the establishment of the Commission...we would like to hold to the term which we had set, mid-1997, July," Jezek told a news conference.

At a meeting on financial market regulation in December, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus dropped his long-held objections to an independent commission but rejected creating regulations which would concentrate trading on any single market.

The finance ministry, which has been criticised for lax regulation of the capital markets, is to transform its market supervision department into a separate and beefed up "Securities Bureau" by the beginning of February.
The prices of trades registered on the SCP are also supposed to be publicly disclosed from February, but details of how this will be conducted have not been released.
